reels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 18

cards.head: In 1544 the English Crown found a tax nobody had to vote for.
The silver in a penny fell from 0.639 grams to 0.108 grams.
The mints struck about £4 million of coin in seven years.
cards.sub: The Crown kept about £1.27 million in profit.

cards.head: Then a 1551 decree halved the face value of the silver coin.
A loan is written in a unit.
cards.sub: In 1551 the unit changed twice between spring and autumn.

end.title: The Great Debasement
end.line: When the Crown taxed the coin itself, 1544 to 1551

reels.caption:
Henry VIII never asked Parliament for this tax. He took it out of the coins.

Between 1544 and 1551 the silver in an English penny fell by 83 percent, the mints struck about £4 million of coin, and the Crown kept roughly £1.27 million. Then a 1551 decree halved the face value of the silver coinage, and the people holding it paid a second time.

reels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 12

cards.head: Tulip mania is finance's favorite bubble story.
cards.sub: The archives tell a smaller one.

cards.head: Ordinary Witte Croonen bulbs rose about 26-fold in January 1637.
cards.sub: Within a week in February they fell to a twentieth of the peak.

cards.head: Most broken contracts settled for 3.5 to 10 percent of the price.
The historian Anne Goldgar found no bankruptcy caused by tulips.
cards.sub: The Dutch economy showed no measurable effect.

cards.head: So where did the legend come from?
cards.sub: The same story machine now writes about memecoins.

reels.caption:
Everyone knows the tulip mania story. The archives know a smaller one.

Prices did spike: ordinary Witte Croonen bulbs rose about 26-fold in January 1637 and lost most of it within a week. But most broken contracts settled for 3.5 to 10 percent of the price, and the historian Anne Goldgar found no bankruptcy caused by tulips.

Episode 12 of The Druid Deep Dive asks how a trade that small became the bubble every bubble is compared to. Full episode on sagix.io, link in bio.

In 1717 John Law ran the bank, the asset and the price.

The Drift attackers rebuilt the same closed loop.

reels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 17

cards.head: The track was real. The traffic was not.
From 1868 to 1873 American railroads laid over 31,000 miles of track.
Around 1870 railroads were 92.6 percent of the bonds listed on US exchanges.
September 20, 1873: the New York Stock Exchange closed for the first time.
cards.sub: It stayed shut for ten days.

cards.head: Between 1873 and 1875, 35.9 percent of the bond market defaulted.
cards.sub: The downturn lasted 65 months, the longest on the NBER's books.

end.title: Railroad bond mania
end.line: The track was real, the traffic was not, 1868 to 1879

reels.caption:
The track was real. The traffic was not.

American railroads laid a little over 31,000 miles of line between 1868 and 1873, almost all of it on borrowed money, and by 1870 railroads made up 92.6 percent of the bonds listed on US exchanges. In September 1873 the New York Stock Exchange closed for the first time, and 35.9 percent of the bond market defaulted over the next three years.

reels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 13

cards.head: October 1923: prices in Germany doubled every 3.7 days.
From January 1922 to August 1923 wholesale prices rose 25,723-fold.
People stopped using the mark.
cards.sub: By November 1923 it was about 7 percent of the money in use.

cards.head: Loans were written in rye, coal, potash, gold and sterling.
The stabilization was built on money people had already chosen.

reels.caption:
In October 1923 German prices doubled every 3.7 days.

People did not wait for a fix. They moved to dollar-indexed private notes, foreign cash and loans written in rye, coal and gold, until the paper mark was about 7 percent of the money in use. The stabilization that followed was built on what they had already chosen.

slides.title: Scotland ran on private banknotes for over a century, with no central bank.

slides.text: Banks in Scotland in 1772 and in 1830. Rival banks issued their own notes, cleared them weekly and held them at par.
Bank failures per thousand banks per year, 1809 to 1830, in Scotland against England.
Counted back to 1772, the rates were 14.88 and 14.90. Sechrest found the difference not significant.
A weekly note exchange, partners liable with their own estates, and London behind them.
Episode 16 checks them against that list. They have the exchange and the delay clause. They have no liability.

carousels.caption:
For more than a century Scotland's money was issued by rival private banks, with no central bank at all.

The notes were cleared weekly and held at par. Between 1809 and 1830 Scottish banks failed at 4.0 per thousand a year against 18.1 in England, though counted back to 1772 the gap disappears, and the episode shows both readings.

carousels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 15

slides.title: The Medici built a bank that no single branch could sink.

slides.text: Florence's partnership system appears. Forty-eight existed in the city before 1400.
Each branch had its own name, capital and books. Branches charged each other commission like strangers.
When a Milanese merchant sued in Bruges, the separation between branches stood.
A branch manager lent twice the branch's capital to a duke. No structure stops that.
Episode 15 reads a Singapore judgment on a cross-chain bridge against the Medici design.

slides.title: The Medici network
slides.line: A holding company with no court above it, 1397 to 1494

carousels.caption:
The Medici bank was not one firm. It was a chain of legally separate partnerships under one name, so that no branch could sink the house.

The design held when a Milanese merchant sued in Bruges. It did nothing when a branch manager lent twice the branch's capital to a duke.

carousels.label: The Druid Deep Dive · Episode 14

slides.title: The day the peg broke: Bretton Woods to the Nixon shock.

slides.text: An ounce of gold, fixed in 1944 by 730 delegates from 44 nations. Every other currency pegged to the dollar within 1 percent.
In 1955 US gold was worth about 160 percent more than official dollars abroad. By 1971 it covered 25 percent of them.
The US payments deficit by August 1971, up from $9 billion in 1970.
The gold window closed "temporarily," with an exception written into the same sentence.
Two devaluations later, in February 1973. Within a month nearly every major currency was floating.

slides.title: The day the peg broke
slides.line: Bretton Woods to the Nixon shock, 1944 to 1973

carousels.caption:
A peg is a promise until someone tests it.

In 1944 the dollar was fixed to gold at $35 an ounce and the world's currencies to the dollar. By 1971 US gold covered about a quarter of the official dollars held abroad, the payments deficit had reached $30 billion, and on August 15 the gold window closed, "temporarily."

slides.title: Is your DeFi position liquid? Pool depth is one quarter of the answer.

slides.text: Is there enough market depth to absorb your exit?
Is there a lender of last resort when confidence breaks? In 2008 the Fed lent nearly $600 billion through swap lines to cover offshore dollars.
Can you move the asset to where depth exists? After Herstatt failed in 1974, interbank transfers fell about 60 percent in three days.
Is there a nexus that connects your asset's market to the others? Rothschild made London that node.

slides.title: The four-layer framework
slides.line: Two hundred years of plumbing failures, one checklist

carousels.caption:
Most DeFi liquidity checks stop at pool depth. That is one quarter of the picture.

The Druid Deep Dive's Episode 9 traced two hundred years of financial plumbing, from Jackson's Bank War to Rothschild's London, and it comes down to four questions: is the pool deep enough, is there a backstop, can the asset move, and is there a hub.
